title: Optical observation of interlayer spin correlation
authors: Akiyoshi Park, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Andrey Grankin, Emil Viñas Boström, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Hassan Alnatah, Masoud Mohammadi-Arzanagh, Gautam Nambiar, Beini Gao, Alireza Alvandi, Sakthi Rajmano Madhan Kumar, Ghadah Alshalan, Isaac Sherwood, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, You Zhou, Arun Ramanathan, Xavier Roy, Angel Rubio, Mohammad Hafezi
abstract: Spin correlations govern numerous collective behaviors of quantum materials, underpinning exotic phenomena such as unconventional superconductivity and topological magnetism. In layered materials, the interlayer spin correlation is important because it characterizes the magnetic ground state and determines spin transport across the interface. Yet interlayer spin correlations have remained hard to measure directly, leaving one of the most basic quantities of two-dimensional magnetism out of experimental reach. Here we provide the first direct optical probe of interlayer spin correlations, using two-magnon Raman scattering in the van der Waals antiferromagnet (AFM) CrSBr, in remarkable agreement with a microscopic spin-wave model without any fitting parameter. Moreover, the two-magnon channel switches on only in the AFM state and vanishes when a magnetic field takes the crystal to a ferromagnetic state. We furthermore establish an exciton-mediated variant of the technique, where tuning the laser near the exciton resonance enhances the signal roughly tenfold due to the exciton's large oscillator strength. Magnon-pair Raman spectroscopy thus opens a direct optical window into interlayer spin correlations in van der Waals magnets, extendable to twisted bilayers and proximity-coupled heterostructures.
summary: This paper introduces two-magnon Raman scattering as a novel, direct optical probe for measuring interlayer spin correlations in layered antiferromagnets. By analyzing the spectral features and observing the signal's collapse under an external magnetic field, the authors confirm that the measured signal originates specifically from the interlayer magnetic bonds. This technique opens a new window into the fundamental magnetic physics of van der Waals magnets.
main_problem: Interlayer spin correlation in layered quantum magnets is crucial for understanding their magnetic ground state and spin transport, but it has been experimentally difficult to measure directly.
main_result: The authors report the first direct optical measurement of interlayer spin correlations using two-magnon Raman scattering in vdW antiferromagnets, confirming its magnetic origin and field dependence.
method: The study combines two-magnon Raman scattering spectroscopy with theoretical modeling based on the Fleury–Loudon interaction to probe the interlayer spin correlation function.
model_or_system: The system is a van der Waals antiferromagnet (AFM) like CrSBr, modeled by a spin Hamiltonian incorporating interlayer exchange coupling. The physics is analyzed using two-magnon continuum theory, which splits into three distinct polarization channels.
key_observables: Two-magnon Raman intensity, which reports the integrated weight of the interlayer bond correlation ($\langle\hat{S}_A \cdot \hat{S}_Bangle$), and its dependence on external magnetic field ($B$).
important_parameters: Interlayer exchange coupling ($J_{z2}$), magnetic field strength ($B$), and the energy gaps associated with optical and acoustic magnon modes (e.g., 46 meV, 82 meV).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Fleury–Loudon light–matter interaction framework and assumes the two-magnon continuum can be accurately decomposed into distinct polarization channels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Raman setup, the theoretical decomposition of the two-magnon spectrum into three channels, and how the measured signal collapses or changes character when the magnetic field drives the system into different magnetic phases (AFM to FM).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical necessity of measuring interlayer spin correlation, introduces the two-magnon Raman scattering technique as the probe, presents the theoretical framework linking the signal to the spin correlation function, and validates the method by showing its sensitivity to the magnetic ordering state via field-dependent measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, non-invasive optical tool (magnon-pair Raman spectroscopy) to probe fundamental, hard-to-measure quantities like interlayer spin correlations in 2D magnets, bridging the gap between theoretical models and experimental observation in strongly correlated systems.
